content: Serious and potentially fatal hypersensitivity reactions have been associated with the use of abacavir-containing products, including EPZICOM. Patients who carry the HLA-B5701 allele are at a significantly higher risk of developing such reactions. It is recommended to screen for the HLA-B5701 allele prior to initiating abacavir therapy, as this has been shown to reduce the risk of hypersensitivity reactions. Screening is also advised before reinitiating abacavir in patients with unknown HLA-B5701 status who have previously tolerated the drug. For patients who test positive for HLA-B5701, treatment with abacavir-containing regimens is not recommended and should only be considered under exceptional circumstances with close medical supervision, where the potential benefits outweigh the risks. Even in HLA-B5701-negative patients, hypersensitivity reactions to abacavir can occur, though less frequently. Regardless of HLA-B5701 status, EPZICOM should be permanently discontinued if hypersensitivity cannot be ruled out, even if other diagnoses are possible. Patients should be educated about the signs and symptoms of hypersensitivity, which typically involve multiple organ systems and may include fever, rash, gastrointestinal symptoms (e.g., nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, or abdominal pain), generalized malaise or fatigue, and respiratory symptoms (e.g., dyspnea, cough, or pharyngitis). Hypersensitivity reactions may occur with a single symptom but are less common. In clinical trials, hypersensitivity reactions to abacavir were reported in approximately 8% of subjects, with symptoms usually appearing within the first six weeks of treatment. The median time to onset was nine days, and 95% of affected individuals reported symptoms from two or more of the five symptom groups. Less common signs include lethargy, myolysis, edema, abnormal chest X-ray findings (e.g., localized infiltrates), and paresthesia. Severe outcomes such as anaphylaxis, liver failure, renal failure, hypotension, respiratory distress, and death have been reported. Rash, when present, is often maculopapular or urticarial but can vary in appearance. Laboratory abnormalities may include elevated liver function tests, creatine phosphokinase, creatinine, and lymphopenia. If a hypersensitivity reaction is suspected, EPZICOM must be discontinued immediately. Reintroduction of abacavir-containing products after a hypersensitivity reaction is strictly contraindicated, as it can lead to more severe symptoms, including life-threatening hypotension and death. If EPZICOM is discontinued for reasons other than hypersensitivity, the reason for discontinuation must be carefully evaluated before considering reinitiation. Patients with unknown HLA-B5701 status should be screened before reinitiating therapy. If hypersensitivity cannot be ruled out, abacavir should not be reintroduced. Even in the absence of the HLA-B5701 allele, abacavir must be permanently discontinued if hypersensitivity is suspected. Lactic acidosis and severe hepatomegaly with steatosis, including fatal cases, have been reported with the use of nucleoside analogues, including abacavir and lamivudine. These events are more common in women, and risk factors include obesity and prolonged nucleoside exposure. EPZICOM should be used with caution in patients with known risk factors for liver disease, though cases have also been reported in patients without such risk factors. Treatment should be suspended in any patient who develops clinical or laboratory findings suggestive of lactic acidosis or pronounced hepatotoxicity, even in the absence of marked transaminase elevations. In patients co-infected with HIV-1 and hepatitis B virus (HBV), discontinuation of lamivudine-containing regimens has been associated with post-treatment exacerbations of hepatitis. These exacerbations, primarily detected by serum ALT elevations and re-emergence of HBV DNA, are usually self-limited but can be fatal. Patients should be closely monitored for several months after stopping treatment. The emergence of lamivudine-resistant HBV has been reported in both HIV-1 and non-HIV-1-infected patients, potentially diminishing treatment efficacy. Patients receiving EPZICOM in combination with interferon alfa and/or ribavirin should be closely monitored for treatment-associated toxicities, particularly hepatic decompensation. Discontinuation of EPZICOM should be considered as medically appropriate in such cases. Immune reconstitution syndrome has been reported in patients treated with combination antiretroviral therapy, including EPZICOM. During the initial phase of treatment, patients may develop an inflammatory response to residual opportunistic infections, necessitating further evaluation and treatment. Autoimmune disorders, such as Graves’ disease, polymyositis, and Guillain-Barré syndrome, have also been reported, with variable onset times, sometimes occurring months after treatment initiation. Fat redistribution and accumulation, including central obesity, dorsocervical fat enlargement (buffalo hump), peripheral wasting, facial wasting, breast enlargement, and a cushingoid appearance, have been observed in patients receiving antiretroviral therapy. The mechanism and long-term consequences of these events are unknown, and a causal relationship has not been established. EPZICOM contains fixed doses of abacavir and lamivudine and should not be administered concomitantly with other abacaviror lamivudine-containing products, such as ZIAGEN, EPIVIR, EPIVIR-HBV, COMBIVIR, or TRIZIVIR, or with emtricitabine-containing products, such as ATRIPLA, EMTRIVA, TRUVADA, or COMPLERA. The complete prescribing information for all agents being considered for use with EPZICOM should be consulted before initiating combination therapy.
